newsitem.title: FRANCE: Smoker sues France's Seita over cancer.
newsitem.headline: Smoker sues France's Seita over cancer.

text.p: A two-pack-a-day Gauloise smoker is suing French tobacco giant Seita, accusing the company of causing his cancer in the first legal case of its kind ever brought in France, his lawyer said on Thursday.
Richard Guerlain, 47, alleges his cancer was caused by smoking Seita's best-selling pungent Gauloises Brunes cigarettes and is claiming 2.7 million francs ($513,000) in damages.
"My client has three types of cancer, he's going to die soon, he's seeking damages," his lawyer Francis Caballero said.
A Seita spokeswoman called the allegations unfounded and said the company was "absolutely confident" about the outcome of the case expected to be heard next summer.
The suit alleges a "persistent and serious failure to inform smokers accurately about the dangers of Gaulloises and its addictive and cancer-causing properties."
The company's flagship Gauloises and Gitanes dark tobacco cigarettes were trademarks of Gallic chic for generations but demand has slipped in recent years in favour of lighter brands.
While a number of high-profile cases have been brought against tobacco companies in the United States, there have only been a handful in Europe.

Last January, an Italian woman sued the Italian government over her husband's 1990 death from lung cancer, claiming it did not warn citizens of the health risk. In Britain, legal firm Leigh Day & Co has said it will sue Imperial Tobacco on behalf of 40 ex-smokers with lung cancer.
Seita, which was privatised last year, said the only similar case ever filed in France was brought against a bank by the family of an employee who died.
The suit claimed she was the victim of passive smoking. The court threw it out last month for lack of legal proof.
French cigarettes started carrying warnings about the health effects of smoking in 1976 and tobacco ads now are banned.

Gourlain, whose family has joined the suit, suffers from tongue and lung cancer and was forced to quit his trade as a butcher because of ill-health. He started smoking filtreless Gauloises at 14 and the suit says he is still "hooked" on them.
The French newspaper Le Parisien quoted his wife as saying the "little blue packets have ruined my life."
Gourlain's case is being funded by the French national anti-tobacco group, Comite National Contre le Tabagisme, whose spokesman Pascal Melihan-Cheinin says it hopes to "put a face on the statistics."
"Young people think you just die right away from this but that's not so," he said. "You can be badly handicapped and dependent."

While the numbers of French smokers has fallen, it is estimated 40 percent of men and 25 percent of women still smoke, Melihan-Cheinin said. The problem is worst among the young, with 60 percent of 18-year-olds puffing cigarettes.
After the suit against Seita was announced, the company's shares slid nearly one percent before retracing most of their losses to close down 0.23 percent at 212.30 francs. ($1=5.258 French Franc)
